<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>High attrition rates constitute a major bottleneck in small-molecule drug discovery, largely arising from poor molecular developability rather than an insufficient pharmacological activity. Drug-likeness, druggability, and molecular developability represent complementary evaluation concepts that address different aspects of small-molecule drug discovery. Nevertheless, inconsistent terminology, fragmented evaluation frameworks, and inherent drawbacks of traditional empirical workflows impair the reliability and applicability of molecular property assessment. As powerful multivariate analytical tools, chemometric methods overcome these limitations and enable quantitative, systematic, and high-throughput molecular property evaluation. This Review clarifies the definitions and relationships among the three concepts and summarizes their classical evaluation approaches. Following the paradigm shift from empirical rules to chemometric modeling, multiobjective optimization, and large-model prediction, advanced computational pipelines are categorized into direct molecular similarity evaluation and predictive modeling of key molecular properties. We discuss the principles, progress, performance, strengths, and limitations of each technical strategy and highlight their synergistic values in lead discovery, structural modification, multiobjective optimization, and focused library design. Finally, challenges for standardized molecular-evaluation systems are analyzed, and future trends of chemometrics-assisted multiobjective optimization and large-model-driven intelligent molecular profiling are prospected.</jats:p>
title:
Drug-Likeness,
Druggability, and Molecular Developability
via Chemometric Evaluation: A Review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Optical interference from small molecules─compounds that absorb UV/visible light or exhibit intrinsic fluorescence─is a significant source of false positives and false negatives in fluorescence- and absorbance-based high-throughput screening assays. Computational prediction of optical activity from molecular structure offers a promising route to early triage of such compounds, yet the problem is challenging due to its quantum mechanical underpinnings and the extreme class imbalance characteristic of diverse drug-like libraries. Here I describe a domain-aware feature engineering and automated hyperparameter optimization approach developed for the EUOS25 Challenge, a benchmark comprising approximately 100,000 small organic compounds with experimentally measured UV/visible absorbance and fluorescence spectra. Beyond standard RDKit physicochemical descriptors and molecular fingerprints, I developed four domain-specific descriptor groups that encode prior chemical knowledge about chromophoric systems: count fingerprints of Murcko scaffolds derived from known dyes and fluorophores, binary indicators for manually curated chromophoric substructures, semiempirical quantum-mechanical descriptors from GFN2-xTB calculations, and ML-predicted quantum properties trained on the QM9 data set. Meta-learning features - probability outputs of baseline models trained on structurally related, easier-to-model end points - were included as cross-task inputs. Hyperparameter optimization was performed using the FLAML automated machine learning framework. The best model for each end point was selected from three complementary strategies: single best model, ensemble consensus, and semisupervised pseudolabeling. Postchallenge feature importance and ablation analyses showed that cross-task meta-features were the dominant driver of predictive accuracy for physically related end points. Semiempirical xTB descriptors─in particular─HOMO–LUMO gap and dipole/quadrupole terms - rank among the top-weighted CatBoost features and provide a physically interpretable account of model behavior. The dye-scaffold and chromophore-indicator descriptors, by contrast, carry genuine but redundant signal: used in isolation they classify well above chance for the two well-predicted end points, yet their removal from the full feature set produces no statistically significant change for any end point, indicating that the fingerprint/2D backbone already encodes this information. These results demonstrate that combining a standard cheminformatics backbone with cross-task meta-learning and automated hyperparameter optimization yields highly competitive predictive models on this benchmark.</jats:p>
title:
Domain-Aware Feature
Engineering for Prediction of
Molecular Optical Interference in High-Throughput Screening

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Protein kinases regulate signal transduction through phosphorylation, and their dysregulation drives diseases like cancer, autoimmune disorders, and Alzheimer’s, making them key drug targets. Fragment-based drug design offers a powerful route to kinase inhibitors but often neglects kinase-specific structural insights. While KinFragLib, a library consisting of 7486 fragments derived from kinase-ligand complexes, provides a rich resource, exhaustive recombination of its fragments is computationally demanding. Here, we present an efficient exploration strategy that integrates subpocket-guided fragment growing with template docking to navigate this vast chemical space. Our automated pipeline prioritizes kinase-specific structural information, enabling targeted generation of chemically diverse ligands. Applied to the PKA kinase, the approach produced 33758 candidate molecules with promising docking scores, of which 15 were synthesized. Seven molecules reduced kinase activity by more than 50% at an inhibitor concentration of 100 μM, and five of these compounds also showed promising efficacy at a concentration of 10 μM. The IC50 determination ultimately revealed that five of the molecules were effective in the two- to three-digit nanomolar range. Crystallographic validation confirmed the predicted binding mode of the most potent compound. This methodology demonstrates how structure-informed guidance can transform fragment-based design into a scalable route for discovering novel kinase inhibitors.</jats:p>
title:
Subpocket-Aware
Fragment-Based Docking Pipeline for
Kinase Ligand Design: Methodology and a PKA Case Study

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The binding affinity of a ligand to a protein is influenced by the protonation and tautomeric states of both partners. However, this relationship remains under-investigated due to the limited availability of computational tools capable of treating charge and tautomer states together in a scalable manner to study clinically relevant systems. Here, we use multi-conformation continuum electrostatics (MCCE) to calculate the protonation and tautomer distributions of nine kinase domains bound to 18 FDA-approved inhibitors across 37 cocrystal structures, while considering their Boltzmann-ensemble. The full pipeline was repeated in triplicate, so that every reported value carries a measured run-to-run uncertainty. Our simulations show that protein net charge and proton distribution remain largely stable even upon binding charged inhibitors. Our results find that individual inhibitor charges are dynamic, frequently increasing or decreasing upon binding a specific protein target. We observe that kinase-inhibitor binding shifts the relative probabilities of low-energy states (ΔG &lt; 2.8 kcal/mol), but does not increase the probability of higher-energy states in the bound form. By considering all low-energy charge states and tautomers, we identify when two solution-state tautomers of nearly equal population resolve upon binding into a single state, creating free energy differences of up to 3.5 kcal/mol between tautomers, and in some complexes differences beyond the resolution of the sampling. In turn, we find that minority species can become the dominant component in the bound state, emphasizing the necessity of considering ensemble-wide protonation and tautomer states to accurately predict protein–ligand binding energetics.</jats:p>
title:
Kinase Inhibitors
can Change Protonation or Tautomeric
State upon Binding
